extras.title: Egypt: Tulunid, Abbasid and Ikhshidid governments
extras.location: Egypt and, at times, neighbouring lands
extras.note: An explicitly grouped transition frame: Tulunids 868–905, restored direct Abbasid government 905–935, and Ikhshidids 935–969; this is not one dynasty.

extras.title: Zagwe dynasty
extras.note: The dynasty’s origins and exact founding date remain uncertain. Christian traditions connect this period with Aksumite and later Ethiopian histories, without establishing an uninterrupted royal genealogy.

extras.title: Ethiopia: post-monarchical eras
extras.note: This groups the Derg, subsequent transitional government and later federal republic. These are different regimes and constitutional orders, not one government lasting from 1974.

extras.title: Eritrea: independent state
extras.note: Independence followed a long war, military victory in 1991 and the 1993 referendum. The modern border is not a boundary inherited unchanged from Aksum.

extras.title: Omani and Zanzibar coastal rule
extras.location: Western Indian Ocean and selected East African coastal ports
extras.note: A regional frame for changing Omani and Zanzibar authority, not a single state covering every Swahili settlement. The independent Zanzibar sultanate dates from the nineteenth century.

extras.title: German East Africa
extras.location: Mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, with changing frontiers
extras.note: German claims began in 1885, and conquest and administrative control developed later. The territory was divided after World War I.

extras.title: Tanganyika under British administration
extras.note: British occupation was followed by a League of Nations mandate and UN trust territory; 1919 is a transition anchor rather than the date of all legal arrangements.

extras.title: Tanganyika: independent state
extras.note: Independence in 1961 was followed by a republic in 1962 and union with Zanzibar in 1964.

extras.title: Zanzibar: independence and revolution
extras.note: Independence under the sultanate in December 1963 was followed by revolution in January 1964 and union in April; these were distinct political stages.

extras.title: United Republic of Tanzania
extras.note: Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on 26 April 1964; Zanzibar retained separate institutions within the union.

extras.title: British East Africa and colonial Kenya
extras.note: A changing colonial frame: protectorate, colony and a legally distinct coastal protectorate; it did not cover every area of British East Africa at all times.

extras.title: Gold Coast, Ashanti, Northern Territories and British Togoland
extras.note: Four different legal territories were administered in relation to the Gold Coast and were joined at independence. Ashanti was not simply annexed to the Gold Coast Colony in 1902.

extras.title: Portuguese Angola
extras.note: Portuguese settlement and claims began centuries before effective conquest of many inland regions. The colonial territory was not identical to the former Kingdom of Kongo.

extras.title: Angola: independent state
extras.note: Independence on 11 November 1975 came amid conflict among nationalist movements and was followed by civil war. This node does not imply the restoration of the Kingdom of Kongo.

extras.title: Cape Colony
extras.note: Dutch settlement began in 1652; British occupation occurred in 1795 and again in 1806. The colony expanded through dispossession, warfare and changing agreements.

extras.title: Colony of Natal
extras.note: A British colony preceding the 1910 Union; its borders and political institutions did not represent all communities of the region.

extras.title: Transvaal Colony
extras.note: British colonial government after conquest of the South African Republic; this node does not date the beginning of societies in the region.

extras.title: Orange River Colony
extras.note: British colonial government following the South African War, before the 1910 Union.

extras.title: South Africa: democratic constitutional era
extras.note: The first national election based on universal adult suffrage was held in April 1994. This is a transition within South African state history, not a new population replacing an earlier one.

maps.title: Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers

connections.label: Trade, migration and conflict
connections.summary: Nubian societies and Egyptian kingdoms exchanged goods and people and fought over access and authority along the Nile.
connections.note: The relationship changed direction over time; neither region was permanently subordinate or culturally uniform.

connections.label: Kushite pharaohs in Egypt
connections.summary: Kushite kings extended their rule into Egypt and formed its Twenty-fifth Dynasty.
connections.note: This selected episode sits within both broad timeline frames; Kushite rule did not begin all Egyptian or Nubian history.

connections.label: Persian conquest of Egypt
connections.summary: Cambyses defeated Egypt’s last Twenty-sixth-Dynasty ruler and brought Egypt into Achaemenid rule.
connections.note: Egypt later regained independence before a second Persian conquest; this was not uninterrupted Persian government until Alexander.

connections.label: Alexander enters Egypt
connections.summary: Alexander took Egypt from Achaemenid control during his campaigns against the Persian Empire.
connections.note: The Persian Empire and Alexander’s campaigns extended far beyond Egypt. Egyptian communities and institutions continued.

connections.label: Ptolemaic kingship
connections.summary: The struggles among Alexander’s successors produced Ptolemaic kingship in Egypt.
connections.note: Ptolemy governed Egypt before adopting the royal title; other successor kingdoms emerged elsewhere.

connections.label: Egypt annexed by Rome
connections.summary: Octavian’s conquest ended Ptolemaic royal government and placed Egypt under Roman administration.
connections.note: Annexation occurred before the conventional imperial starting date of 27 BCE. Roman government did not end Egyptian culture.

connections.label: Eastern Roman government
connections.summary: Egypt remained within the Roman state as its eastern imperial administration centred on Constantinople.
connections.note: This is overlapping periodisation within a continuing empire, not an Egyptian state newly founded or a clean cultural break in 330 or 395.

connections.label: Arab-Muslim conquest
connections.summary: Arab-Muslim armies conquered Byzantine Egypt and established government based at Fustat.
connections.note: Military and administrative change did not cause immediate universal conversion; Coptic Christian communities continued.

connections.label: Egypt under Umayyad rule
connections.summary: Egypt became a province of the Damascus-based Umayyad caliphate.
connections.note: This was a change of ruling authority within the early Islamic state, not the origin of Egypt’s population or all its traditions.

connections.label: Abbasid provincial rule
connections.summary: The Abbasid revolution brought Egypt under the new caliphal dynasty.
connections.note: Egypt’s provincial connection should not be read as uninterrupted direct Baghdad control throughout the Abbasid period.

connections.label: Autonomous and restored governments
connections.summary: Egypt passed through Tulunid government, restored direct Abbasid rule and Ikhshidid government.
connections.note: These are three successive arrangements grouped in one explicitly labelled transition frame, with continuing Abbasid religious allegiance.

connections.label: Fatimids conquer Egypt
connections.summary: Fatimid forces took Egypt and established Cairo, later making it their capital.
connections.note: The Fatimid caliphate began in North Africa in 909; 969 dates its Egyptian expansion rather than the foundation of the dynasty.

connections.label: Saladin ends Fatimid rule
connections.summary: Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate and established Ayyubid government in Egypt.
connections.note: A political and religious reorientation did not replace all inhabitants or erase Fatimid institutions and artistic traditions.

connections.label: Mamluks take power in Egypt
connections.summary: Mamluk leaders overthrew the last independent Ayyubid sultan in Egypt and established their own sultanate.
connections.note: Ayyubid branches continued in Syria and elsewhere; the Egyptian event does not end every Ayyubid polity in 1250.

connections.label: Ottoman conquest
connections.summary: Ottoman campaigns defeated the Mamluk sultanate and incorporated Syria and Egypt into the Ottoman Empire.
connections.note: Mamluk elites and institutions persisted after the sultanate ended; Ottoman rule had regional variation.

connections.label: Muhammad Ali appointed
connections.summary: Muhammad Ali became Ottoman governor of Egypt in 1805 and founded a dynasty whose hereditary rule was formally recognised in 1841.
connections.note: This followed French occupation and renewed Ottoman intervention; growing Egyptian autonomy did not immediately end Ottoman suzerainty.

connections.label: British occupation
connections.summary: Britain occupied Egypt while the Muhammad Ali dynasty remained in office.
connections.note: Occupation, dynastic rule and Ottoman suzerainty overlapped; Britain declared a protectorate only in 1914.

connections.label: Limited independence recognised
connections.summary: Britain ended its formal protectorate and recognised Egypt as a sovereign state while reserving several matters for later agreement.
connections.note: British military presence and restrictions remained; this was not complete immediate withdrawal.

connections.label: Monarchy ends; republic declared
connections.summary: The 1952 revolution was followed by abolition of the monarchy and proclamation of a republic in 1953.
connections.note: The destination frame begins with limited independence in 1922 and includes this later constitutional rupture; the two timeline blocks intentionally overlap.

connections.label: Augustus and imperial government
connections.summary: Octavian received the title Augustus as Roman government took the form conventionally called the Principate.
connections.note: The conventional start of the Roman Empire did not create a new Egyptian population or end every republican institution.

maps.title: Horn of Africa and the Indian Ocean coast

connections.label: Trade and Christian networks
connections.summary: Aksum and the eastern Roman world participated in commercial, religious and artistic networks across the Red Sea and eastern Mediterranean.
connections.note: Contact did not mean Aksum was a Byzantine province or that African Christianity had only one origin.

connections.label: Later highland Christian kingdoms
connections.summary: Later highland kingdoms including the Zagwe preserved and developed Christian traditions after Aksumite political power declined.
connections.note: The intervening political sequence is incompletely known: this is a qualified cultural and regional connection, not proven unbroken dynastic succession.

connections.label: Solomonic dynasty takes power
connections.summary: Yekuno Amlak displaced Zagwe rule and established the dynasty conventionally called Solomonic.
connections.note: The dynasty’s claim to descend from biblical Solomon is a legitimising tradition, not an independently demonstrated genealogy.

connections.label: Monarchy overthrown
connections.summary: The Derg deposed Haile Selassie and replaced imperial government with military rule.
connections.note: This begins a broad post-monarchical frame containing later changes of regime, not a single uninterrupted republic.

connections.label: Eritrean independence
connections.summary: Eritrean military victory and a UN-supervised referendum led to recognised independence from Ethiopia.
connections.note: Ethiopia continued as a state; the modern Eritrean border and independence process are not a simple redivision of ancient Aksum.

connections.label: Gold and Indian Ocean trade
connections.summary: Great Zimbabwe was connected through long-distance trade to the Indian Ocean coast, with Kilwa coins among its imported finds.
connections.note: Goods travelled through networks and intermediaries; an imported coin is not proof that Great Zimbabwe was ruled by Kilwa or that every shipment went directly between the two cities.

connections.label: Portuguese fort and occupation
connections.summary: Portuguese forces established a fort at Kilwa during their expansion along the East African coast.
connections.note: Their occupation was limited and contested; the Portuguese kingdom did not originate in Kilwa, and Swahili communities continued.

connections.label: Omani and Zanzibar authority
connections.summary: Omani Busaidi rulers based in Zanzibar later exercised authority at Kilwa and adapted its buildings for their administration.
connections.note: This selected later episode follows intervening local histories; coastal authority varied and does not imply all Swahili cities formed one uninterrupted empire.

connections.label: German mainland expansion
connections.summary: German colonial expansion displaced local authorities and acquired control of mainland coastal jurisdictions associated with Zanzibar.
connections.note: The mainland and island sultanate had different legal histories; Zanzibar itself did not become part of German East Africa.

connections.label: Postwar partition and mandate
connections.summary: The postwar division of German East Africa placed the mainland territory later called Tanganyika under British administration.
connections.note: Rwanda and Burundi went to Belgian administration and the Kionga Triangle to Portugal; Tanganyika was only one successor jurisdiction.

connections.label: Tanganyika independent
connections.summary: Tanganyika became independent from British administration.
connections.note: It became a republic in 1962 before union with Zanzibar; the event does not date the beginning of its peoples or communities.

connections.label: Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite
connections.summary: Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined to form the union later named Tanzania.
connections.note: Zanzibar retained institutions within the union; its independence in 1963 and revolution in January 1964 preceded the agreement.

connections.label: Coastal protectorate administered
connections.summary: Britain administered the Sultan of Zanzibar’s mainland coastal protectorate together with colonial Kenya.
connections.note: The coastal protectorate had a legal status distinct from the inland colony until independence; the edge does not place all Zanzibar under Kenyan government.

connections.label: Kenya independent
connections.summary: Kenya became independent of British rule and the separate coastal arrangement ended.
connections.note: A republic followed in 1964; the modern state joined regions with diverse earlier histories.

connections.label: Independence and revolution
connections.summary: Zanzibar became independent under a sultanate before the January 1964 revolution replaced the monarchy with a republic.
connections.note: This concerns the islands and their government, not all territories formerly influenced by Omani or Zanzibar rulers along the mainland coast.

maps.title: Sahel, Yoruba cities and the Gold Coast

connections.label: Changing Sahelian centres
connections.summary: Mali rose within western Sahelian trading and political networks that had earlier sustained Ghana/Wagadu.
connections.note: This is regional reconfiguration, not proof that Ghana uniformly merged into Mali on one date; Ghana’s decline and Mali’s expansion were uneven.

connections.label: Inland Niger urban networks
connections.summary: Jenne-jeno and the surrounding Inland Niger Delta formed part of the commercial and political landscape of the Mali era.
connections.note: The archaeological city and later Jenne are distinct settlements; urban communities had their own histories and were not created by imperial conquest.

connections.label: Later Jenne under Songhai
connections.summary: Songhai expanded its authority over the Inland Niger Delta and later Jenne after the main occupation phase of Jenne-jeno.
connections.note: The plotted Jenne-jeno block ends around 1400; this link explicitly follows the neighbouring city and regional urban history rather than claiming the old settlement remained the same imperial capital.

connections.label: Royal traditions connect Yoruba cities
connections.summary: Ife and Oyo are linked in Yoruba royal traditions associated with Oranmiyan.
connections.note: Oral dynastic traditions are not proof that Oyo simply descended as a state from Ife; the Oyo timeline selects its much later imperial expansion.

connections.label: Niger-to-Ife trade routes
connections.summary: Oyo channelled goods from Niger-region trading networks towards Ife and other Yoruba centres.
connections.note: This concerns the city’s earlier commercial history rather than dating the beginning of the imperial expansion block; no political merger is implied.

connections.label: Asante annexation
connections.summary: Britain annexed Asante and established colonial government under an official responsible to the Gold Coast governor.
connections.note: Ashanti had a separate colonial legal status, and the Asante monarchy and communities continued; this was not annexation to the Gold Coast Colony itself.

connections.label: Ghana independent
connections.summary: The Gold Coast, Ashanti, Northern Territories and British Togoland became independent as Ghana.
connections.note: The four territories had different legal histories; modern Ghana is geographically and politically distinct from medieval Ghana/Wagadu.

connections.label: Archaeological heritage, not succession
connections.summary: Nok terracottas discovered in central Nigeria became part of the archaeological and museum heritage of modern Nigeria.
connections.note: This is a heritage and geographical link only: there is no established direct dynastic succession from Nok culture to the Nigerian state or to a named later kingdom. The discovery began before independence.

connections.label: One jurisdiction within the wider era
connections.summary: Colonial Nigeria is one specific British jurisdiction within the atlas’s broader African colonial-period overview.
connections.note: This is a period-to-example relationship, not a merger or a claim that all Africa had the same rulers or independence date.

maps.title: Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states

connections.label: Diplomacy and Christian exchange
connections.summary: Portuguese contact with Kongo led to diplomacy and religious and artistic exchanges between their rulers and communities.
connections.note: Early contact did not mean immediate Portuguese conquest or an equal relationship throughout later centuries; the slave trade and colonial warfare transformed the relationship.

connections.label: Colonial expansion in the Kongo region
connections.summary: Portuguese colonial expansion absorbed the southern Kongo region into Angola as Kongo political authority weakened.
connections.note: This shows only the Angolan branch: Kongo communities also live in both modern Congos, and the colonial territory was not simply the old kingdom renamed. No claim is made that all Kongo lands passed to Portugal.

connections.label: Angola independent
connections.summary: Portuguese rule ended as Angola became independent amid fighting between rival nationalist movements.
connections.note: This was not a peaceful agreed merger or the restoration of Kongo; independence was followed by civil war.

connections.label: Mbanza Kongo: living heritage
connections.summary: The former Kongo capital, Mbanza Kongo, survives as a cultural and spiritual heritage site in present-day Angola.
connections.note: A heritage link is not a claim that Angola alone inherits Kongo peoples, culture or territory.

connections.label: British occupation of the Cape
connections.summary: Britain occupied the Cape during wars with European rivals and retained control after its second occupation.
connections.note: The Cape settlement began under Dutch rule in 1652, and colonial expansion involved African dispossession and resistance.

connections.label: Four colonies form the Union
connections.summary: The Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies joined in the Union of South Africa.
connections.note: The Union was a self-governing British dominion dominated by white political power and excluded most South Africans; this was not universal democratic unification.

connections.label: Transition to universal suffrage
connections.summary: South Africa held its first national democratic election based on universal adult suffrage under an interim constitution.
connections.note: This was a constitutional and political transformation within the state; earlier segregation and apartheid are not equivalent to the later democratic order.

connections.label: Different paths out of colonial rule
connections.summary: Ghana, Kenya and Angola illustrate separate decolonisation processes in different years and colonial systems.
connections.note: The starting box is a broad era, not a state that split into these three countries; these are examples, not an exhaustive list of African independence movements.

editorialNotes: Heritage and period-to-example links explicitly mark context rather than political succession; render them dashed and label their basis. Nok has no invented direct dynastic successor.
The Jenne-jeno node deliberately distinguishes the old archaeological settlement from nearby later Jenne.

Egyptian rule maps selected transitions, not every dynasty or brief interruption; Achaemenid independence interruptions, Coptic continuity, Tulunid/Ikhshidid stages and the overlapping Muhammad Ali/British/modern frames are named.
For continuity to existing Sahel and Nigerian endpoints, retain existing west-africa and africa-modern maps and offer cross-map links at shared nodes.
Every proposed claim is grounded in the source URLs. The two Yoruba traditional links remain marked as tradition or historical contact; they are not asserted as genetic descent.
